name: symbol-table-for-nested-scopes
intent: Track every declaration in the scope that introduces it and resolve each name from the innermost enclosing scope outward, so shadowing is explicit, names bind to the declaration the language says they do, and name lookup stays a separate phase from syntax recognition.
problem: Once a language can nest scopes - blocks inside functions inside modules, classes inside classes, loops, catch clauses and comprehensions that each introduce their own region - a name no longer identifies one declaration: the same spelling may be declared in several scopes, and every use must bind to the innermost declaration that precedes it. A single flat table (or a map per file) either merges those declarations, reports false duplicates, or resolves a shadowed name to the wrong one; and if lookup is scattered through the parser, the confusion is duplicated in every later phase, so the type checker, the code generator, the diagnostics, rename and go-to-definition all disagree about what the name means.
context: Compiler, interpreter, linter, formatter or language-server front ends for languages with lexical nesting - the situation Parr frames as grouping symbols into scopes and resolving them (Language Implementation Patterns ch. 6, pattern 17) and Nystrom works through for a block-structured language in 'Resolving and Binding' (Crafting Interpreters ch. 11). It applies when declarations and uses are separated in the program text (blocks, functions, classes, modules, let-bindings, nested DSL sections), when shadowing is legal, and when later phases need to know which declaration a use denotes - typically as a define-then-resolve pair of passes over an AST.
benefits: Shadowing becomes explicit and correct: the innermost enclosing declaration wins, an outer declaration is reachable again once the inner scope closes, and the rule is implemented once instead of guessed at every use site.

Separation of concerns: syntax recognition stays in the parser and name binding in a dedicated resolver, so the two evolve independently and the resolver can be tested against a fixture tree without a parser.

One mechanism serves every scope-establishing construct - blocks, functions, parameters, classes, modules, loops, catch clauses, comprehension and type-parameter scopes - because they all reduce to the same define/lookup primitives.

Later phases work with symbol identity rather than spelling: type checking, code generation, refactoring and diagnostics address the resolved symbol (or a fixed scope distance), so they never repeat the lookup or re-invent shadowing.

Diagnostics improve: duplicate declarations are reported in the one scope that owns them, unresolved names carry their position, and use-before-declaration or self-referential initializers become explicit findings instead of silent misbindings.

Precomputed bindings remove a class of runtime bugs: storing the resolution (scope distance, de Bruijn index or symbol reference) on the use site makes name access independent of when code runs - exactly the closure bug Nystrom's resolver fixes.
tradeoffs: Two passes (or an explicit declared-but-not-yet-defined state) are needed: a single define-as-you-parse table cannot handle forward references, mutual recursion or circular type definitions, so declaration order and hoisting rules must be designed deliberately rather than inherited from traversal order.

The scope tree duplicates structure the AST already has: every construct that establishes a scope must be recognised in the walk, and one that is missed (a catch clause, a comprehension, a class scope that does not enclose methods, Swift's sequential scopes, C labels) silently resolves names under the wrong policy.

Storage is a real fork with different failure modes: per-scope hash tables allocate per block, while a single table plus a shadow stack is cheaper but its restore-on-exit step is easy to get wrong and leaves stale bindings behind.

Symbol lifetime must be decided up front: symbols kept for later phases have to outlive the resolution pass (arena or explicit ownership), and freeing scopes eagerly makes any retained pointer dangle.

Languages with several name spaces (values, types, macros, labels) need one table per namespace per scope; collapsing them into one map produces false duplicate definitions and lets a type name resolve to a value.

The structure is a snapshot: in an editor or REPL the source keeps changing, so the tree must be rebuilt or made persistent/incremental - and a mutable scope object shared with a closure changes meaning after later declarations, which is the bug Nystrom demonstrates.
Cached resolutions are only valid while the tree they came from is valid; a refactoring that moves a declaration invalidates every stored scope distance and forces the pass to run again.

participants.responsibility: One entry per declaration: name, kind, the declaration node it came from, its owning scope and the flags later phases need (defined vs merely declared, parameter/local/global, namespace).

The namespace of one region: an entry map keyed by name (or an equivalent open-addressed table), a link to the enclosing scope, and the operations define (insert and detect duplicates) and lookup-here; scope kind and source extent are recorded so diagnostics and later passes can address it.
The explicit representation of nesting - a parent link per scope or a stack of open scopes maintained while walking the tree - which fixes the search order: innermost outward, first match wins.

Walks the tree and defines every symbol in the scope that owns it, applying the language's hoisting and declaration-order rules and rejecting duplicate declarations within one scope while allowing shadowing across scopes.

Walks the tree again (or the same walk when one pass suffices) and resolves every identifier use innermost-outward, storing the result on the use site - scope distance, de Bruijn index or direct symbol reference - and reporting names that resolve nowhere.
Where the language separates kinds of names (terms, types, macros, labels, struct members), one table per namespace per scope; resolution consults the namespace the syntactic position demands.
Collects duplicate-declaration, use-before-definition, shadowing and unresolved-name findings with positions, so one bad name does not abort the whole analysis.

use_cases: Programming-language front ends: block, function, class and module scoping in compilers and interpreters, from Parr's Cymbol and Nystrom's Lox to production front ends.

DSL and configuration languages with nested sections or let-bindings - call descriptions, policy languages, query languages with subqueries, template languages with loop or with scopes - where the same name may be rebound in an inner section.
Linters, formatters, refactoring tools and language servers: unused-variable detection, rename, go-to-definition and scope-aware formatting all need the binding from each use to its declaration.
Type checkers and other semantic analysers that bind names before deriving types, effects or macros, using the define-then-resolve split so annotations and forward references work.
Interpreters that resolve once and execute many times, keeping the binding (scope distance or slot index) on the use site so runtime access is not a chain walk - the fix that makes closures behave.
Embedded scripting layers and REPLs where each module, class or block introduces a namespace that must shadow outer ones, and each additional evaluation session starts from a fresh root scope.

Go's go/types type checker implements the pattern directly: every region is a types.Scope holding its declarations with a link to its parent scope, and the documented Scope.LookupParent operation is the innermost-outward walk that binds each identifier during checking - the same scope graph powers go-to-definition and rename in editor tooling.

CPython's compiler builds a tree of symbol tables, one SymbolTable per module, function or class scope (published as the symtable module), marking each identifier bound or free in that scope so name access compiles to a direct local lookup or closure-cell dereference instead of a runtime chain walk.

The TypeScript compiler splits the work exactly this way: the binder walks the AST once and fills a SymbolTable per container (function, block, module - locals and exports, with duplicate-identifier detection) before the checker resolves names against those tables, so checking, emit and editor services share one binding decision.
avoid_when: The format has no nesting and no shadowing - flat key=value configuration, INI-like files, single-namespace record schemas: a plain map from name to value is the whole solution.

The language is dynamically scoped, or name binding is deliberately deferred to runtime (early Lisp dialects, some shell and template evaluation models): an environment chain with dynamic lookup is the honest model, and a static scope tree answers a different question.
Nothing downstream consumes the binding - pure syntax highlighting, format conversion, transclusion or tokenisation: do not build and resolve a symbol model nobody reads.

You are writing a tool for a language whose compiler already exposes its symbol model (Roslyn SemanticModel, go/types Scope, Python's symtable, javac's Trees, the TypeScript checker, swift-syntax's lookup): use that instead of re-deriving resolution rules you must then track forever.

All names live in one global scope (a tiny DSL with no blocks or nested declarations): the monolithic-scope form of the table is enough, and the scope tree adds bookkeeping without changing behaviour.

Lookup really is by user-supplied name at runtime (reflection, eval, dynamic property access, metaprogramming-heavy runtimes): a static table is at best a partial view, and forcing names into it produces false unresolved-name findings.
anti_patterns: A single flat table for a nested language, patched with name mangling (prefixes like block$name) or last-writer-wins insertion: shadowed declarations silently collapse and diagnostics point at the wrong declaration.
Resolving names inside the parser's rule functions, so scope handling is scattered through syntax code and duplicated by every later phase that needs a binding.

Rebuilding resolution at runtime by walking the environment chain on every access, which is slow and, with a mutable chain, wrong for closures (Crafting Interpreters ch. 11 opens with exactly that bug).
Treating 'declared' and 'defined' as one flag: self-referential initializers (var x = x), forward references and hoisted functions then resolve to the wrong thing or crash.
One table mixing several name spaces (values, types, macros, labels), producing false duplicate-definition errors and resolving a type name to a value.
Keeping the scope tree as a second source of truth that drifts from the AST: when a construct is added to the syntax but not to the walk, resolution silently uses the enclosing scope.
Sharing one mutable resolver (or one scope stack) across files, threads or REPL sessions, making results order-dependent.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: syntax recognition and name binding are different phases; the resolver consumes the tree the parser produced and never re-parses.
Explicit representation: nesting is data (an enclosing-scope link or an explicit stack of open scopes), not a naming convention and not an implicit property of traversal order.

The lexical scope rule is encoded once: a use refers to the preceding declaration with the same name in the innermost enclosing scope - shadowing is legal, redeclaration in the same scope is an error.
Single source of truth per symbol: later phases address the symbol (or its fixed slot/distance), not the spelling, so name resolution happens once.
Encapsulation of the table: callers see define/lookup operations, not the entry storage, so the container can change (hash table, shadow stack, arena) without touching callers.
Model the language's actual scoping policy explicitly - hoisting, block versus function scope, non-local declarations, separate name spaces - instead of assuming one generic rule.
best_practices: Split definition and resolution (or make the declared-but-not-defined state explicit) so forward references, mutual recursion and self-referential initializers are handled deliberately.

Create a fresh scope for every scope-establishing construct and keep the stack discipline (push on enter, pop on exit) with exactly one current scope; if scopes must outlive the walk, keep them in an arena instead of freeing them.
Store the resolution result on the use site - scope distance, de Bruijn index or symbol reference - so later phases never re-search and runtime access never walks a chain.
Report duplicates at definition time (within one scope only; shadowing across scopes is legal) and unresolved names at resolution time, always with source positions.
Model one table per namespace where the language has separate name spaces (types versus terms versus macros; labels; struct members) and resolve according to the syntactic position.
Keep the resolver free of I/O and of downstream semantics: type inference, macro expansion and code generation are later phases that consume the bindings.
Confine resolver state to one compilation and one thread; if bindings are published to other threads, publish them read-only.

Test with fixtures for shadowing depth, same-scope redeclaration, use-before-declaration, unresolved names and namespace separation, asserting the resolved distance or symbol - not merely that resolution did not crash.
sources: Parr, T., Language Implementation Patterns: Create Your Own Domain-Specific and General Programming Languages (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2010), ch. 6 Tracking and Identifying Program Symbols - sections 6.2 Grouping Symbols into Scopes and 6.3 Resolving Symbols, with Pattern 17 Symbol Table for Nested Scopes (p. 163) and the monolithic-scope contrast in Pattern 16.

Nystrom, R., Crafting Interpreters (2021), ch. 11 Resolving and Binding - a stack with one map per scope, shadowing, the closure bug caused by resolving through a mutable environment chain, and precomputed scope distances.

Aho, A. V., Lam, M. S., Sethi, R. & Ullman, J. D., Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, 2nd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2006), section 2.7 Symbol Tables - a symbol table per scope, scope entry and exit, shadowing and lookup.
